EXP-000 · Cartesia Fig. 7 re-analysis

2026-10-28 · status: done · cost: $0 · script: logbook/exp000_reference.py

Question. How much of the blog's ">10x fewer tokens" comes from the architecture, and how much from comparing a cooled-down H-Net with a stable-phase SmolLM3?

Data. The per-checkpoint scores behind blog I Fig. 7, extracted from the page's chart bundle into configs/reference/blog1_fig7_{hnet,smollm3}.csv: * the H-Net has 154 points to 0.99T tokens (cooldown from 0.855T); * SmolLM3 has 117 points to 11.04T (stage 1 up to 7.93T).

The six tasks are HellaSwag, ARC, PIQA, WinoGrande, CSQA and MMLU.

Method. Fit SmolLM3's stage-1 (stable-LR) average as a quadratic in log tokens. For each stable-phase H-Net point, find the SmolLM3 token count that reaches the same score.

Results.

H-Net tokens H-Net avg SmolLM3 avg at same tokens SmolLM3 tokens to match (smoothed) Data multiplier
94B 55.66 53.87 162B 1.7x
189B 58.11 56.86 560B 3.0x
301B 58.74 — 822B 2.7x
0.99T (after cooldown) 63.82 — 11.04T (SmolLM3 final, after stages 2–3) 11x

Takeaways. * The architecture effect at matched stable phase is real but ~2–3x, not 10x. The H-Net's cooldown adds ~2.3 points (61.5 → 63.8). * Our pass criteria for any H-Net vs baseline comparison use stable-vs-stable multipliers. Cooldown is a separate, explicitly labelled branch. * Cartesia's SmolLM3 Winogrande (63.69 at the end) differs from the model card (58.88), so their eval setup differs from the card. Our harness is validated against these CSV numbers, not the card.

EXP-001 · What the blog's chunk-viewer data says about the improved router

2026-10-28 · status: done · cost: $0 · scripts: scripts/reference/parse_chunk_viewer.py, scripts/reference/analyze_chunk_viewer.py, logbook/exp001_chunk_viewer.py

Question. The blog's H-Net is unreleased and differs from the paper's (which the blog calls "LH-Net", lazy/lookahead). What does its router actually do?

Data. Blog I Figs. 10–11 are interactive viewers. Their data files hold 96 texts (45 natural-language, 51 code) with, for each text: * the improved H-Net's stage-0/1 boundary positions and per-byte boundary probabilities p; * LH-Net's boundaries on the same texts; * Llama-3 and in-corpus BPE tokenizations.

These were parsed as data (no page code was executed) into configs/reference/chunk_viewer.json. The viewer code labels an improved-H-Net boundary byte "ends here" (ends: true on every example) and a trailing chunk without one "unfinished".

Results. * End-of-chunk boundaries. p ≥ 0.5 coincides with "this byte is the last byte of a stage-0 chunk" on 99.76% of 327,081 bytes. The decision at byte t can only use bytes ≤ t, so there is no lookahead. * Spaces go at the end of chunks. 92% (English), 78% (other languages) and 68% (code) of stage-1 chunks end right after a space. LH-Net and BPE attach the space to the next word instead (≤ 20%). * Clean stage-1 units.

Stage-1 cuts English Other languages CJK
Inside a word: improved H-Net 0% 0.5% —
Inside a word: LH-Net 3% 3% —
Inside a UTF-8 character: improved H-Net 0% 0.01% 0.5%
Inside a UTF-8 character: LH-Net 3% 24% 81%
Inside a UTF-8 character: Llama-3 BPE 0.2% 0.07% 4%

This confirms the blog's CJK claim quantitatively. * Compression (bytes per stage-1 chunk):

Model English Other languages CJK Code
Improved H-Net 7.0 9.7 4.3 7.0
LH-Net 7.4 7.0 3.6 7.4
Llama-3 BPE 4.5 4.5 3.6 4.0
  • Boundary probabilities are bimodal (most mass below 0.1 or above 0.9), with a tail in between.

Example (first 96 bytes of the English example, ␣ = space):

H-Net s0 : Ever␣|wonder|ed␣|if␣|you|␣|could␣|beat|␣|a␣|bear|␣|or␣|a␣|horse|␣|in␣|a␣|race|?|␣|What|␣|about␣|a␣|rat␣|or␣|a␣|rh|ino|?|␣|The␣|an
H-Net s1 : Ever␣|wondered␣|if␣|you␣could␣|beat␣|a␣bear␣|or␣|a␣horse␣|in␣|a␣race?␣|What␣|about␣|a␣rat␣|or␣|a␣rhino?␣|The␣|an
LH-Net s0: Ever|␣wondered|␣i|f␣you|␣could|␣be|at|␣a|␣be|ar|␣or|␣a|␣ho|rse|␣i|n␣a|␣ra|ce|?␣|What|␣about|␣a|␣rat|␣or|␣a|␣r|hino|?␣|The|␣an
LH-Net s1: Ever|␣wondered|␣i|f␣you␣could␣beat|␣a␣bear|␣or|␣a␣horse|␣in␣a|␣race|?␣What|␣about|␣a␣rat|␣or|␣a␣rhino|?␣The␣an
Llama-3  : Ever|␣wondered|␣if|␣you|␣could|␣beat|␣a|␣bear|␣or|␣a|␣horse|␣in|␣a|␣race|?|␣What|␣about|␣a|␣rat|␣or|␣a|␣rh|ino|?|␣The|␣an

What we implement from this. * Routers declare start or end boundary semantics. * With end semantics, the chunk vector is the last byte's state, and byte t reads the most recent chunk that ended at or before t. * The router function is still a guess. Candidates end_linear, end_mlp and end_cosine_shift go through the 1–10M architecture search (PLAN §2b), with the chunk statistics above as the targets for our trained models.

EXP-002 · Tiny architecture search: routers and ablations vs BPE

2026-10-29 · status: done · hardware: spot L4s (GCP), 3 runs in parallel per VM · spec: configs/search/exp002_tiny2m.yaml · commits f988ba8 … 9e9f8c4 · fairness: runs/search/exp002_tiny2m/fairness.md

Question. At tiny scale and equal FLOPs/byte and data: * does the paper's 2-stage H-Net beat the BPE baseline; * does an end-of-chunk router (the blog's design, EXP-001) beat the paper's lookahead router; * which paper components matter?

Setup. Nine variants, each with 2 seeds. * Baseline: BPE (GPT-2 tokenizer, 15M params incl. a 50K-vocab head). * H-Nets (~7.9M params, 2-stage, (3,3)), with these routers: * the paper's cosine_lookahead; * three end-of-chunk guesses: end_linear, end_mlp and end_cosine_shift. * Ablations of the paper router: * targets (4,2); * no smoothing; * no per-stage LR multipliers; * ratio-loss α = 0.1.

All runs share: * Data: FineWeb-Edu train shard 1 in the same window order; 231M bytes per run (50M token-equivalents). * Optimizer: AdamW, peak LR 1.5e-3, WSD (10% warmup, 20% inverse-sqrt decay), bf16, no compile. * Evaluation: the same 1 MB val text for bpb, plus paper7 task metrics every 500 steps.

Results (all 18 runs done; logbook/tables/exp002_summary.md, figure re-rendered by logbook/exp002_progress.py).

variant val bpb (2 seeds) realized compute vs budget
BPE baseline 1.635 0%
paper router (LH-Net) 1.78–1.80 +7% to +12%
end-of-chunk MLP 1.78–1.81 +3%
end-of-chunk cosine / linear 1.79–1.85
ablations (targets 4/2, no smoothing, no LR multipliers, α 0.1) 1.82–1.84
  • Every H-Net trails BPE by 0.15–0.21 bpb at this ~2M-parameter scale; the variants differ by less than the seed spread (up to 0.05), so EXP-002 cannot rank routers or ablations. Three seeds from EXP-003 on.
  • All H-Nets show a transient early router collapse (stage 1 up to ~300 bytes/position) that recovers by ~10M bytes; the paper-router runs then settle ~7% below their target compression, i.e. over the FLOPs budget (found later; see the realized-compute note under EXP-010).
  • Two infrastructure bugs were found and fixed on the way: a CUDA illegal memory access in flex attention's compiled block-mask builder on per-step packed lengths, and a thread-safety race in Triton's autotuner when two post-run diagnostics ran at once.

Mechanism study (between EXP-002 and the fix sweeps)

Tools: hnet/analysis/diagnose.py, probe_texts.py, probe_main.py, main_signal.py; a per-step probe run (logbook/figures/probe_dynamics.png); details and tables in logbook/WORKLOG.md.

  1. The hierarchy is barely used. Zeroing the innermost main network (6.0M of 7.9M params, 38% of FLOPs) costs 0.04 bpb; zeroing everything below stage 0 costs 0.69. The main network's gradient norm drops to 1–3% of stage 0's within 20 steps in every variant.
  2. Why (per-step probe run): the residual bypass starts at zero, so at init the decoder sees only the untrained hierarchy; the stage-0 router switches it off (47 bytes/chunk by step 20) and the main network's gradient falls 17×; the ratio loss forces compression back, stage 1 collapses in turn, and by step 80 the residual path has overtaken the hierarchy signal. From then on the stage-1 router drifts to coin flips (46–70% of p in 0.4–0.6).
  3. The chunk vector is a boundary state, not a chunk summary. Probes on the main network's input: with the end-of-chunk router it encodes the chunk's last byte almost losslessly (0.18 bits) but its first byte barely (3.3–3.6 of 4.8 bits left, even with an MLP probe). The main network does not know which word it sees. With the paper's start semantics the vector encodes the first byte and nothing of the chunk (a one-chunk lag).
  4. Not a decoder bottleneck, not a noisy gradient. The main network's output is less predictive than its input (2.62 vs 2.08 bits), and its gradient SNR at the training batch is normal (2.4 at step 500 vs 1.9 for stage 0).
  5. 84% of the gap to BPE (token-aligned on identical text) is in the letters of "space+word" tokens: word identity.
  6. Routers run over budget. The LM loss pulls every router toward more boundaries (dCE/dshift < 0 at stage 0 in all models); the α = 0.03 ratio loss pushes back 2.5–4× more weakly, so compression settles 10–16% above the FLOPs budget. At stage 1 both gradients are ~1e-4: the router is unconstrained, and at lr ≥ 3e-3 it becomes a limit cycle between select-all and select-none (logbook/figures/exp003_collapses.png).
  7. Neither model copies in context at ~50M tokens (repeated phrases still cost ~2 bits/byte): this regime is for mechanisms, not for the final verdict.

EXP-003 · AdamW learning-rate sweep (tuned fairness)

spec configs/search/exp003_lr_adamw.yaml · 4 architectures × LR {5e-4 … 6e-3} × 3 seeds = 60 runs · status: ~40/60 done · partial report logbook/reports/exp003_partial/

Result so far. BPE's best LR is 6e-3, at the grid edge (1.564 ± 0.012); every H-Net peaks at 1.5e-3 (1.78–1.80) and degrades above it because of the stage-1 limit cycle (finding 6). At tuned settings the gap is 0.235 bpb, not 0.17. The paper's LR multipliers put stage 0 at 3.5× base and the main network at 0.72×.

EXP-006 · Parameter matching with hashed n-gram embeddings

spec configs/search/exp006_close_gap_tiny.yaml · BPE vs 1-/2-stage H-Net ± FLOP-free n-gram tables matching BPE's 15M parameters · 3 seeds · status: ~12/18 done

arm val bpb realized compute
BPE 1.634 ± 0.002
2-stage paper router 1.795 (1 seed) +11.7%
2-stage + n-gram 1.714 ± 0.016 +1.2%
1-stage learned router 1.845 ± 0.002 +5.8%
1-stage + n-gram 1.705 (1 seed) +0.7%

Finding. ~40% of the gap is BPE's free vocabulary table. But the gain lands in the byte stage (punctuation, word-internal bytes), not in the hierarchy: the main network's contribution drops (0.63 → 0.38 bpb).

EXP-009 · Oracle chunking: is routing the bottleneck?

spec configs/search/exp009_oracle_chunks.yaml · 1-stage H-Net with hand-made boundaries at identical FLOPs · 3 seeds · status: done

boundaries (6 bytes/chunk) val bpb main-network contribution
fixed every 6 bytes 1.859 ± 0.007 0.25
learned (EXP-006 hnet1) 1.845 ± 0.002
oracle word starts 1.827 ± 0.006 0.45
oracle word ends 1.806 ± 0.026 0.56

Finding. Chunk semantics decide how much the hierarchy is used (end > start > fixed), but even oracle word chunks are only 0.04 better than the learned router and 0.17 behind BPE: routing is not the main gap here.

EXP-008 · Training signals for the hierarchy (paper router) · EXP-011 · the same with fixed (3,3) pooling

specs exp008_hierarchy_use.yaml, exp011_fixed_hourglass.yaml · residual path-drop, main-path auxiliary head, router-entropy penalty, identity-init residual, residual warmup · 3 seeds · status: running

So far (1 seed each): path-drop alone hurts (1.895; hierarchy dead); the aux head alone is marginal (1.821 vs 1.823); the entropy penalty is harmful: it drives the routers to select almost everything (combo_end reached 1.652 at +379% FLOPs, i.e. invalid, and the paper-router combo ran out of memory the same way). Both combo arms were dropped from the spec.

EXP-010 · Dynamics fixes and Mamba-free outer networks

spec exp010_dynamics_and_mixers.yaml · strong ratio loss (α 1), identity residual, both; outer Mamba-2 replaced by sliding-window attention (+1.1% FLOPs) or Kimi Delta Attention (+0.3%) · 3 seeds · status: running (the KDA arm first failed on a kernel channel-count constraint, fixed)

So far: alpha1 1.818 at +0.8% compute: the strong ratio loss holds compression, and the paper router's apparent edge over fixed chunks (1.823) was extra compute. resid_id 1.783 but at +15.6% compute.

EXP-014 · Rank-based (quantile) boundary decisions

spec exp014_quantile_decision.yaml · hnet/model/routing/decide.py: select the top 1/N positions by p (batch quantile, running threshold for eval, p recentred so the threshold is 0.5). Compression is pinned exactly and the ratio loss becomes inert. Arms: quantile, quantile + attention pooling, each at lr 1.5e-3 and 6e-3 · 3 seeds · status: stopped at step ~500, invalid (see work log: the p-space quantile saturated and collapsed the selection in most runs; the decider was rewritten to rank batch-normalized fp32 logits and is validated as the quant_fix arm of EXP-017). EXP-015/016 were built on the same rule and were stopped with it; they will be re-run on the fixed rule only if EXP-017 says the hierarchy is worth more training signals.

EXP-017 · A vocabulary for the learned chunks (learned tokenization with a token table)

spec exp017_chunk_vocab.yaml · hnet/model/chunk_vocab.py · 2-stage (3,3), end-of-chunk MLP router, rank decisions, lr 1.5e-3, EXP-002 budget · arms: quant_fix (fixed rank decisions, no vocabulary), vocab (each stage-0 chunk's byte content hashed by 2 hashes into 65536-row tables, 12.6M parameters ≈ BPE's 12.9M embedding + head, zero FLOPs, added to the chunk vector), vocab_pred / vocab_pred_w1 (plus a sampled-softmax next-chunk objective for the main network, 1024 candidates, +1.6% FLOPs, weight 0.5 / 1.0) · 3 seeds · status: launching

Hypothesis: the gap to BPE is word identity, which BPE stores in a FLOP-free table and the H-Net must compute; and the main network gets no word-level training signal. A hashed vocabulary over the router's chunks gives both, and makes the segmentation matter (a chunk's identity is its token), which is what a learned tokenizer needs to be trained on.

EXP-018 · Where should the chunk vocabulary sit? (1-stage, word-scale chunks)

spec exp018_vocab_shapes.yaml · 1-stage H-Net (ratio 6, chunks ≈ words), end-of-chunk MLP router, rank decisions · arms h1_quant (no vocabulary), h1_vocab_pred (vocabulary + next-chunk prediction) · 3 seeds · status: done: h1_quant 1.853 (1.854/1.861/1.845); h1_vocab_pred 1.720 / 1.863 / 1.737, main-network contribution 0.75 / 0.13 / 0.55 bpb (baseline 0.13–0.17). Two seeds: −0.13 / −0.11 bpb at identical FLOPs, best honest-compute H-Net so far; seed 1 did not adopt the hierarchy (heavy-tailed router scores → confidences ≈ 0.5 → residual path wins; fixed by the robust decider, EXP-021).

EXP-019 · A router that is a tokenizer: context-free boundary scores

spec exp019_local_router.yaml · hnet/model/routing/local.py (local_mlp: logit from the last 8 bytes only, so the same string is always cut the same way) + rank decisions · arms local, local_vocab, local_vocab_pred (same vocabulary arms as EXP-017, which uses the contextual end_mlp router) · 3 seeds · status: running

Motivation: chunk_stats on trained routers (work log): stage-1 chunks are 48–55% singletons and recurring words are segmented consistently only 23–53% of the time. Prediction: local* arms score far higher on consistency; if the vocabulary then helps more than in EXP-017, consistency is the missing ingredient of learned tokenization.

EXP-020 · Router self-consistency penalty (second launch, scale-free)

spec exp020_router_consistency.yaml · 2-stage (3,3), end_mlp, rank decisions · penalty = within-4-gram-group variance / total variance of the stage-0 logit · arms cons1, cons10, cons10_vocab_pred · 3 seeds · status: cons1 1.768 / 1.812 / 1.813 → 1.798, cons10 1.775 / 1.783 / 1.840 → 1.799, vs EXP-017 quant_fix 1.799 ± 0.005: neutral on average with a larger seed spread (two seeds −0.02, one +0.04); main-network contribution 0.02–0.06 (baseline 0.03). cons10_vocab_pred pending. Consistency can be imposed on a character-pair tokenizer without cost, but it does not by itself make the second level useful at (3,3); the word-scale line (EXP-018/023) is where the gain is.

EXP-021 · (stopped) word-scale vocabulary with the median/MAD decider

Stopped at step ~1000: the MAD of a word tokenizer's boundary scores is ~0 (5/6 identical "not a boundary" logits), 1/σ blew up the gradient and seed 0 diverged (work log). Replaced by EXP-023.

spec exp023_word_vocab_trimmed.yaml · 1-stage ratio 6, end_mlp, rank decisions on trimmed-standardized scores, chunk vocabulary (2 × 65536 × 96) + next-chunk objective (w 0.5, 1024 candidates) · 3 seeds · baseline EXP-018 h1_quant 1.853 · status: vp and vp_ng done, vp_rwarm finishing

arm val bpb (s0 / s1 / s2) main-network contribution vs baseline
vp vocabulary + prediction 1.732 / 1.855 / 1.733 0.72 / 0.18 / 0.64 −0.12 / 0.00 / −0.11
vp_ng + byte n-gram tables 1.720 / 1.669 / 1.656 0.09 / 0.41 / 0.42 BPE is 1.634 ± 0.002

  • vp replicates EXP-018 seed by seed, including the non-adoption of seed 1 with a different decider: adoption is decided by the seed's initialization / data order, early (steps 200–600), not by the score-scale pathology.
  • vp_ng: the adopted seeds are 0.02–0.035 bpb from BPE at identical training FLOPs, with a learned word tokenizer and a main network that carries 0.42 bpb. The two parameter-side memories are complementary: n-gram tables give the byte stage local identity, the chunk table gives the hierarchy word identity.

Root cause of the EXP-002 crashes: flex attention mask builder, not mamba_ssm (commit after 88237a3)

  • Repro on debug VM hnet-ssddbg2, five cases run one at a time with CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1: paper_mb16_s1 aborted (rc 134); the other four passed, including paper_mb16_s0, which had crashed on VM b. The crash is intermittent.
  • With synchronous launches the faulting kernel is the inductor-compiled create_block_mask (_compile=True, deprecated) at attn.py:98, in the main network's attention. The mamba_ssm backward frame in the VM b logs was only where the asynchronous error surfaced.
  • Inner-stage lengths change every step and are almost never a multiple of 128. During the transient early router collapse (stage 1 reaching up to ~300 bytes/position) they are very short, about one position per document.
  • VM c then hit the same crash in paper_nolrmult_s1 and paper_nosmooth_s1, so it isn't specific to one VM or variant.
  • Fix: attn.packed_block_mask. It builds the mask eagerly and clamps the mask_mod indices to T−1, using a tensor bound so flex does not recompile when T changes. It is used by attn, NSA, DSA and MoBA.
  • Regression test: flex vs SDPA on ragged packed lengths (tests/test_flex_mask.py). Full suite: 584 passed.
  • Verification on GPU: hnet-ssddbg3 runs paper s0–s3 and end_linear s0–s1.
  • Also found: every healthy H-Net run shows the transient early collapse (it recovers to target by ~10M bytes). To look at after EXP-002: ratio-loss warmup or a lower stage-0 LR multiplier during warmup.

  • It can now be added as an EXP-005 variant, e.g. --set model.attn_res=[0,0,2] for the main network only.

Deep dive: what the tiny H-Net learns, and why it trails BPE

Tools: hnet/analysis/diagnose.py (per-byte loss by byte class and chunk position, router confidence, boundary alignment, zero-main ablations, a token-aligned comparison with BPE) and hnet/analysis/probe_texts.py (HTML view of chunks, loss and main-network help on contrasting inputs: logbook/figures/probe_texts.html). Per-checkpoint JSON is in logbook/diagnostics/. Findings on EXP-002 (paper 2-stage (3,3), final checkpoint, 64–128 val docs): 1. The deepest network is barely used. - Zeroing the innermost main network (6.0M of 7.9M params, 38% of FLOPs) costs 0.04 bpb (paper_s0) or 0.06 (end_mlp_s1). - Zeroing everything below stage 0 costs 0.69, mostly from the stage-1 encoder and decoder. - Over training the main network's help grows only 0.008 → 0.018 → 0.040 (steps 500, 1000, final). 2. The main network's gradient collapses early in every variant. Its gradient norm drops from 7–23% of stage 0's at step 10 to 1–3% by step 20 and stays there. This includes end-of-chunk routers, which never show the early compression spike (up to 104 bytes/chunk at step 20 for the paper router). The decoders learn to rely on the (zero-init) residual path almost immediately. 3. The stage-1 paper router never leaves its initialization. - 46–70% of p sit in 0.4–0.6, and only 2% are confident. - With identity q/k on near-random states, cos ≈ 0 gives p ≈ 0.5 at init. - The ratio loss gives no push either: ∂L/∂G = N/(N−1)·(N·F − 1) = 0 once F is on target. - The only remaining signals (EMA and STE paths) scale with the main network's usefulness, so routing and the main network are stuck in a self-reinforcing equilibrium. - Stage-1 chunk starts after whitespace: 13% (Cartesia's improved H-Net: 92%). 4. The end-of-chunk MLP router does learn word-like chunks: 72% of stage-1 starts follow whitespace, and 67% of stage-0 decisions are confident. Yet the main network's help only rises from 0.04 to 0.06 bpb, and bpb improves by just 0.01. Better chunks alone don't unlock the hierarchy here. 5. Where the gap to BPE is (token-aligned, identical text). 84% of it is in "space+word" GPT-2 tokens, spent on the letters after the space (1.78 bits/byte) rather than the space itself (0.45 bits): word identity. The main network's help goes to newlines (1.3 bits saved), punctuation (0.4) and digits, but only 0.03 bits at word starts. 6. Scale check: neither model copies in context. Repeated phrases cost ~2.1–2.4 bits/byte on the 4th–6th repetition, for BPE as well (no induction heads at ~50M tokens). The tiny regime is dominated by local statistics, where BPE's 13M lookup and head parameters are worth more than any hierarchy. Tiny runs are for debugging mechanisms, not for judging H-Net vs BPE. - Hypotheses for 4–5: a decoder bottleneck (word-level knowledge must be spelled out through a d=96, 4-layer byte decoder and a 256-way head, while BPE has a 6.4M-param word-level head), plus missing capacity at tiny scale. - Running: - EXP-008 (residual path-drop / main-path aux head / router entropy / combined, 3 seeds); - EXP-009 (oracle word chunks vs fixed vs learned at matched FLOPs); - EXP-006 (n-gram embeddings); - a dense-checkpoint probe run for steps 1–400.

Linear probes on the main network: it is not a decoder bottleneck (hnet/analysis/probe_main.py)

Question: does the innermost main network compute next-chunk information that the byte decoder cannot spell out (a decoder bottleneck), or does it compute nothing useful (a training-signal problem)? Multinomial logistic probes on the main network's input x and output z at every innermost position, target = the byte after the chunk's anchor, 70/30 split, held-out bits (logbook/diagnostics/probe_main_*.json):

model positions unigram probe on main INPUT x probe on main OUTPUT z probe on [x, z] model's own loss on those bytes
paper_s0 35.7k 3.98 2.08 2.62 2.03 1.45
end_mlp_s1 37.3k 4.92 3.71 3.89 3.66 3.22
  • The main network's output is less linearly predictive of the next byte than its own input (2.62 vs 2.08 bits for paper_s0; 3.89 vs 3.71 for end_mlp_s1). A 7-layer, 6M-parameter Transformer destroys information its input already carried. Concatenating x and z recovers only ~0.05 bits over x alone.
  • So the hierarchy is not computing next-chunk predictions that the decoder then fails to use. It is simply not trained: this is consistent with the gradient-norm collapse (main-network grad ≈ 1–3% of stage 0's from step 20) and the 0.04-bpb zero-main ablation. The decoder bottleneck hypothesis (item 5 above) is not supported for the main network; the gap to BPE at word starts is mostly a capacity/signal problem at the chunk level.
  • Implication: fixes must deliver gradient to the main network early (bottleneck-first residual warmup, main-path auxiliary head; EXP-008/011) rather than widen the decoder.
  • Caveat: the end_mlp probe targets differ (end-of-chunk anchor → the first byte of the next chunk, a harder, higher-entropy target: unigram 4.92 vs 3.98), so the two rows are not comparable to each other, only within row.

Finding: the chunk vector is a boundary state, not a chunk summary (probe_main.py --identity)

Probes from the innermost main network's input x (the chunk vector) to the bytes of the chunk it represents, on 27–33k held-out positions (logbook/diagnostics/probe_identity_*.json):

model (semantics) target unigram linear from x MLP from x linear from z (main output)
paper_s0 (start) first byte of its chunk 4.83 0.46 – 1.61
paper_s0 (start) last byte of its chunk 4.41 4.11 – 4.13
end_mlp_s1 (end) last byte of its chunk 2.01 0.18 0.08 0.58
end_mlp_s1 (end) first byte of its chunk 4.76 3.60 3.26 3.81
end_mlp_s1 (end) second byte 4.21 3.32 2.99 3.48
end_mlp_s1 (end) chunk length (1–16) 3.64 2.95 2.51 3.07
  • The vector handed to the main network is the encoder's residual-stream state at the boundary byte. It encodes that byte almost losslessly and the rest of the chunk barely (only ~1.5 of 4.8 bits about the first byte of a ~9-byte chunk, even with a nonlinear probe). The main network does not know which word it is looking at, so it cannot do word-level language modelling, which is where the whole gap to BPE sits (84% of the gap is in the letters of "space+word" tokens). The BPE model's input, by contrast, is the token's identity.
  • With the paper's "start" semantics the vector encodes the chunk's first byte and nothing of its content, which can only arrive one chunk later: a built-in one-chunk lag for within-chunk prediction.
  • Also: the main network's output z encodes less of everything than its input (the 7-layer stack destroys the identity information it was given), and its gradient SNR at the training batch size is normal (2.4 at step 500 vs 1.9 for stage 0; main_signal.py), so this is not a noisy-gradient problem: the main network is trained on a signal that contains little word identity.
  • Fix to test next: a pooling chunker. The chunk vector becomes a learned summary over all bytes of the chunk (mean or attention pooling of encoder states within the chunk, plus the boundary state), so the main network's input carries the chunk's identity. This is BLT's byte→patch cross-attention in H-Net clothing, and it is natural only with "end" semantics (the chunk must be complete when its vector is formed).

experiment arm n val bpb main-network contribution (zero-main cost)

  1. Parameter matching is real: FLOP-free n-gram tables (matching BPE's 15M total params) remove ~40% of the gap (0.21 → 0.07 for 1-stage). Cartesia's ladder matches the outer networks to BPE's embedding + head in params AND FLOPs; this is what that buys at tiny scale.
  2. Chunk semantics change how much the hierarchy is used: oracle word-end chunks make the main network worth 0.56 bpb vs 0.25 with fixed chunks; "end" beats "start" by 0.11 of main-network contribution (the lag).
  3. Routing is not the main gap: oracle word chunks are only 0.04 better than the learned router and still 0.17 behind BPE. What remains is what the main network receives (chunk identity: EXP-012) and how early it gets trained (EXP-008/011).

Where the n-gram gain lands; LR sweep; mid-training router collapses

  • n-gram embeddings help the byte stage, not the hierarchy (diagnose.py on EXP-006 hnet1 vs hnet1_ng, same 96 docs): bpb 1.790 → 1.676, but the main network's contribution falls from 0.63 to 0.38 bpb; the gains are in punctuation (gap 0.56 → 0.16) and word-internal bytes. The tables are a BPE-like local-statistics crutch.
  • EXP-003 (partial, 34/60 done): BPE's best LR is 6e-3 at the grid edge (1.564 ± 0.012); every H-Net peaks at 1.5e-3 (1.78–1.80) and degrades above. At tuned settings the gap is 0.235 bpb, not 0.17. Note the paper's LR multipliers put stage 0 at 3.5× base (5.3e-3 at base 1.5e-3) and the main network at 0.72× base (1.1e-3).
  • Mid-training router collapses at LR ≥ 3e-3: stage-1 compression spikes to 18–631 bytes/position for tens of steps (end_mlp lr 6e-3 s0 at step 550; end_cosine_shift lr 3e-3 s1 at step 340), then the ratio loss pulls it back at a cost of ~0.05 bpb. The stage-1 router sits at p ≈ 0.5 (no signal keeps it decided), so a large update can flip a whole batch to "no boundaries". This is the mechanism behind H-Net's LR ceiling.
  • Next: EXP-013 tests whether stabilizing the router (strong ratio loss, entropy penalty) lets the H-Net use BPE's LR, and whether the main network is under-trained (inverted multipliers [1, 1, 4]).

The stage-1 router is a limit cycle at high LR (logbook/figures/exp003_collapses.png)

  • At lr 6e-3 the stage-1 router oscillates for the whole run between compression 1 (every position selected) and ~500 (none), every few steps; at 3e-3 in bursts; at 1.5e-3 it holds near 3. Stage 0 is stable at every LR.
  • Training bpb barely reacts, because the decoder relies on the residual path: nothing damps the router.
  • Mechanism: the ratio loss constrains only the mean of p; the stage-1 p's are clustered near 0.5 (the "undecided router" of the diagnostics), so a uniform shift of the router's bias flips every position at once. The ratio loss then pushes back and Adam's momentum overshoots.
  • The EXP-008 combo OOMs (both seeds) are the same failure: the router-entropy penalty drove the stage-1 router to select everything, the main network saw ~32k positions instead of ~3.6k, and attention ran out of memory. The entropy penalty amplifies the all-flip mode; verdict: harmful.
  • Fix to test: rank-based (quantile) boundary decisions. In training, select the top 1/N positions by p (batch quantile) and keep a running threshold for eval (BatchNorm-style); p is recentred so the threshold maps to 0.5 for the STE and the EMA dechunker. Compression is pinned exactly, the decision is immune to uniform shifts, and the ratio loss becomes an exact constant (inert), so α disappears.

Realized compute: the paper router runs 10–16% over its FLOPs budget (logbook/sweep_summary.py)

The fairness gate checks the configured ratios. Recomputing training FLOPs/byte from each run's realized compression (last 10 logged steps):

arm realized vs budget val bpb
2-stage paper router, α 0.03 (EXP-006 paper, EXP-008 base, EXP-010 resid_id) +10.5% to +15.6% 1.78–1.80
same with strong ratio loss α 1.0 (EXP-010 alpha1) +0.8% 1.818
fixed (3,3) pooling, oracle word chunks, n-gram arms +0.2% to +1.2%
EXP-008 combo_end (router-entropy penalty) +379% (compression 1.15 / 1.54) 1.652: invalid
  • The CE gradient always favours more positions (more compute); at α = 0.03 the ratio loss cannot hold them (its maximum penalty is N·α ≈ 0.09 nats). The paper router's apparent 0.03-bpb edge over fixed chunks was extra compute. EXP-002's paper-router runs were likewise ~7% over budget (2.8/8.5 bytes per position instead of 3/9).
  • combo_end was not a result: the entropy penalty drove both routers to "select almost everything". It does show what the hierarchy can do when it gets positions and training signal, which is the point of the next sweep.
  • Policy from here: H-Net arms use rank (quantile) decisions, which pin compression exactly, or α ≥ 1; every summary reports realized FLOPs vs budget and flags > 2%.

Interim readouts of EXP-008/010/011 (honest-compute view; logbook/sweep_summary.py)

arm val bpb realized compute main-network contribution
paper router, strong ratio loss (α 1) 1.810 ± 0.012 (2 seeds) +0.8% 0.065
paper router, residual path-drop 0.3 1.846 +31% 0.053
paper router, entropy penalty 1.921 +6.6% 0.000
fixed pooling, identity-init residual 1.862 +0.2% 0.000
fixed pooling (zero-init residual) 1.823 +0.2% 0.059
  • Path-drop makes the decoder lean on the hierarchy, which makes the LM loss's pull on the router stronger: the model answers by selecting 31% more positions. Any fix that makes the hierarchy useful inflates compression unless compression is pinned (quantile decisions, EXP-014/015/016).
  • Identity-init residual: the bypass is strong from step 0 and the decoder never uses the hierarchy (contribution 0.000, worse than zero-init). Zero-init starves the hierarchy early; identity-init starves it for good. The hierarchy needs a window where it is necessary but not noise: residual warmup (EXP-011 fixed_rwarm, pending).
  • Entropy penalty: kills the stage-1 hierarchy outright (contribution 0.000) even where it does not collapse compression. Dropped from further use.
  • New intervention (EXP-016): chunk-level multi-byte prediction, a head on the innermost main network's output predicting the next chunk's first k bytes, bypassing dechunker, residual and decoder.

EXP-014 post-mortem: the p-space quantile rule saturates and collapses

metrics.jsonl of the stopped runs: tau/s1 climbs to 1.000 within 70–90 steps, then compression/s1 jumps to 440–600 (only forced boundaries) and stays there (quant__lr0.0015_s1, quant__lr0.006_s0, ...); in quant__lr0.0015_s2 the same happens at stage 0 at step ~290 (compression/s0 1300–1800, then stage 1 selects everything because it sees no free positions). The one healthy-looking run had tau/s0 = 1.000 too.

Mechanism: the quantile threshold was detached, so nothing anchored the scale of the router's logits; the STE confidence gradient pushes selected logits up and unselected ones down forever (the same force that makes the paper router over-select, now with no ratio loss to oppose it). Once logits exceed ~17, sigmoid is exactly 1.0 in fp32 for more than 1/N of the positions, the quantile sits on the tie, recentring gives p' = 0.5 for all of them, the strict > selects none, and the stage is dead (no selected positions → no gradient → no recovery).

Fix (routing/decide.py, tests test_quantile_decision.py): rank the router's raw fp32 logit (RouterOutput.logit) with topk (ties broken by rank, never "none"); standardize the scores over the batch in the graph (BatchNorm style) before the threshold and the confidence, which makes the gradient's common-shift and common-scale components exactly zero (unit test), so the logits cannot inflate; midpoint threshold between the k-th and (k+1)-th score; running mean/std/threshold for eval; temp controls the confidence margins; score_std/s* is logged as the drift diagnostic. A general lesson for H-Net routers: any decision rule needs a scale anchor; the paper's is the ratio loss (weak), ours is normalization.

Zooming out: the hierarchy needs a vocabulary (EXP-017)

The user asked for coarser-grained ideas and reminded that the point of H-Net is learned tokenization. Reading the findings as one story: (1) 84% of the gap to BPE is word identity; (2) BPE gets it from a FLOP-free 12.9M-parameter table, the H-Net has to compute it; (3) the main network receives the boundary byte's state, not the chunk's identity, and gets no word-level training signal; (4) oracle word boundaries barely move bpb, so routing quality is not the bottleneck at this scale: what the main network is fed and trained on is. EXP-017 treats the router's chunks as tokens: hashed chunk-content embeddings (parameter-matched to BPE, zero FLOPs) enter the main network, and a sampled-softmax next-chunk objective trains it. This also makes the segmentation matter to the loss (a chunk's identity is its token), so the learned tokenizer finally has something to be good at. Router-dynamics work stops here; the remaining budget (~$120 of the $200 cap) goes to this line.

What tokenizer did the router learn? (hnet/analysis/chunk_stats.py, 128 val docs, 127 kB)

Three fully trained 2-stage runs (paper cosine router EXP-008 base; end-of-chunk MLP router EXP-003 end_mlp at lr 1.5e-3; paper router at lr 6e-3 EXP-013 lr6_nomult) against a whitespace tokenizer on the same text (logbook/diagnostics/cs_*.json):

segmentation bytes/chunk types / chunks singleton chunks boundaries on word boundaries word types segmented the same way every time
whitespace 6.1 0.35 25% 100% 100%
stage 0, paper router 2.7 0.18 12% 17% 67%
stage 0, end_mlp 2.6 0.15 9% 3% 73%
stage 0, paper lr 6e-3 2.7 0.17 12% 19% 82%
stage 1, paper router 8.0 0.53 48% 14% 53%
stage 1, end_mlp 7.7 0.62 55% 7% 30%
stage 1, paper lr 6e-3 7.8 0.58 52% 17% 23%
  • Stage 0 learns a character-pair tokenizer: the most frequent chunks are single letters and punctuation (' ', e, ,, s, .), and almost no boundary sits on a word boundary (3–19%, vs 44% of word boundaries hit at best). This is the level that the chunk vocabulary of EXP-017 sits on: it will behave like a character bigram/trigram table (useful, cf. the n-gram tables, but it cannot carry word identity).
  • Stage 1 is not a tokenizer: half of its chunks are strings that occur once in 127 kB, and a word seen 3+ times is segmented the same way only 23–53% of the time. The innermost main network therefore sees mostly unique "tokens". No embedding table, no auxiliary loss and no capacity can give it word identity under this segmentation: this is the mechanism behind "main output less predictive than its input" and the 0.04-bpb contribution.
  • The paper's end-to-end router objective (CE through the STE confidence + a ratio loss) contains nothing that rewards consistency: the router is free to place boundaries by context, and it does. A vocabulary needs types.
  • Consequences: (i) EXP-018's 1-stage ratio-6 shape is the right place for a vocabulary (word-scale chunks, but only if they recur); (ii) next: routers that are consistent by construction, a context-free router whose score is a function of the last k bytes only (the same string is always cut the same way, like BPE), and a surprise router (boundary where the model's own next-byte entropy is high, the BLT patching rule) — both as scores for the rank decider, so compression stays pinned; measured with chunk_stats before looking at bpb.

Consistency at initialization vs after training: the router objective is anti-tokenizer

chunk_stats on freshly initialized models (96 val docs): the contextual end_mlp router starts out 92–95% consistent (a recurring word is cut the same way almost every time: a random Mamba encoder has short memory, so its state at a byte is a near-function of the last few bytes), while the trained end_mlp is 73% (stage 0) / 30% (stage 1). Training removes consistency: the CE-through-STE signal rewards boundaries that help prediction in context, never agreement across contexts. The context-free local_mlp is, counter-intuitively, less consistent at init (8% at k = 8, 32% at k = 4): an 8-byte window reaches into the previous word, so the same word gets different scores after different predecessors; a tokenizer is a function of the current chunk's string, not of a fixed window. (EXP-019 stays as the cheap test of whether training fixes this; its windowed design is not the answer.)

Direct answer (new, dc.router_consistency_weight): a self-consistency regularizer on the byte-level router, the variance of its logit across all positions in the batch that end in the same n = 4 bytes (hashed group means via index_add, differentiable, negligible cost). The router keeps its context, but is pulled to agree with itself: the same string → the same decision, which is what gives the hierarchy types to work with.

EXP-020 first launch invalid: an unnormalized consistency penalty is satisfied by shrinking the logits

cons1_s0 metrics: router_consistency/s0 falls to 0.000 while score_std/s0 falls 1.2 → 0.15 (the baseline's rises to 3.9). Under rank decisions on normalized scores the forward pass is invariant to the logit scale, so the cheapest way to zero a within-group variance is to make every logit (nearly) the same constant: the penalty bound nothing. Lesson (same family as the EXP-014 drift, mirrored): once decisions are scale-free, every auxiliary term on the router must be scale-free too. Fix: penalty = within-group variance / total variance (1 − R² of the 4-gram as a predictor of the logit); relaunched as EXP-020 (second launch, same arms).

At word scale (ratio 6) the same component gives −0.09 and −0.05 bpb at step 1000 in two seeds and the main network's contribution rises from 0.13 to 0.56 bpb: the hierarchy carries the model for the first time in this project.

Standardizing by a std that a few outliers dominate puts every other confidence at ≈ 0.5; the EMA dechunker then smooths with P ≈ 0.5, the hierarchy's output stays weak (dechunk_rms 0.65–0.93 vs 1.4–1.6 while residual_rms is 2.1) and the decoder commits to the residual path: the same "residual wins the race" failure as in EXP-002, now with a measurable trigger. Fix: median/MAD standardization with clipped z (default of the rank decider, unit test reproduces the failure mode) → EXP-021.

Give the router's chunks an identity (a table keyed by their content) and a token-level objective, and the second level has something to learn; compression pinning (rank decisions) is what makes the comparison honest.

  • Given a vocabulary and a chunk-level objective, the router converged to a word tokenizer by itself: every word boundary is a chunk boundary and the same word is always one token. That is the learned tokenization H-Net promised, obtained without heuristics, and it is what let the main network take over 0.75 bpb of the work.
  • The non-adopted seed learned a morphological tokenizer (suffixes ing/ed/ly/ion/ment/ation as tokens, cuts before the space): also a consistent segmentation (87%), but more fragmented (37% singletons) and slower to make the hierarchy useful; the residual path won the race first. Both outcomes are reachable from the same objective: adoption is decided early (step 200–600), by whether the hierarchy's signal reaches the decoder before the residual path consolidates. That is the next dynamics problem (EXP-021 removes one trigger, the heavy-tailed-score damping).

EXP-021 (median/MAD decider) stopped: the MAD collapses under a word tokenizer

h1r_vocab_pred_s0: from step ~650 the robust scale score_std/s0 falls 4.4 → 0.0 while p_margin pins at 0.50; grad norm 0.3 → 4.6e3 (step 900) → 1.9e6 (step 1050), val bpb 3.25 at step 1000. With a word tokenizer 5/6 of the positions are "not a boundary" and get near-identical logits, so the median and the MAD both sit inside that mode and the MAD → 0; the ±4 clip protects the forward pass, not the gradient through 1/σ. Seeds 1–2 did not diverge but did not adopt the hierarchy either (1.98 / 2.00 at step 1000 ≈ baseline). h1r_quant ≡ h1_quant (the decider change is invisible without a vocabulary), h1r_vocab_pred_ng reached 1.82 at step 1000 (= paper_ng) before the stop. Fix: mean/std over the central 98% of the scores (outlier-proof, cannot collapse unless 98% of scores coincide; unit test with 5/6 identical scores). Rule, stated generally: a scale estimator for boundary scores must straddle both modes of a bimodal distribution; medians do not. → EXP-023 (same arms + residual warmup; EXP-022 draft superseded).

EXP-023 tokenizer statistics: adoption and the kind of tokenizer go together (cs_exp023_*.json)

checkpoint bpb main contribution boundaries on word boundaries words cut consistently top chunks
vp_ng_s2 (adopted) 1.656 0.42 95% 99.4% the, of, and, to, a
vp_s1 (not adopted) 1.855 0.18 4% 89% s, d, ing, ed, er, ly, ion, ment

Same picture as EXP-018 with the same seed: the seed that ends up with a suffix/morpheme tokenizer is the one whose hierarchy is not adopted; the seeds that find the word tokenizer are adopted and reach 1.66–1.73. Deterministic per seed across two deciders, so the bifurcation is in the router's initialization or the first few hundred steps of data, not in the decision rule. Open question whether the tokenizer causes the non-adoption (morpheme chunks are less predictable, a weaker chunk-level signal) or both follow from the same early state; either way the fix is to steer the first ~300 steps (residual warmup vp_rwarm, pending; or a brief whitespace-prior on the router).
